perseverance.name: Perseverance
perseverance.intro: An ancient lake. A vanished river. Rocks that may preserve a world we have never known. In Jezero Crater, a six-wheeled laboratory investigates Mars’ past and collects samples for possible study on Earth.
perseverance.heroAlt: NASA’s Perseverance rover on the surface of Mars

status.title: On the surface of Mars
status.body: Landed on 18 February 2021. This page explores the mission’s science and landmark sites; the map is an illustration, not the rover’s current position.

stats.label: Rover mass
stats.note: About the size of a small car

exploration.title: Four clues to an ancient world
exploration.intro: Choose a numbered location to explore the questions behind the mission. Follow the story from the crater floor to the rocks along its rim.
exploration.description: Illustrative map of Jezero Crater with its river delta, landing area, sample depot and crater rim
exploration.note: Conceptual map: positions, route, relief and distances are simplified. These are selected scientific landmarks, not a live traverse map.

stops.name: Crater floor
stops.body: The rover landed inside a 45-kilometre-wide impact crater. Some floor rocks formed from magma, then interacted with water: a record of both volcanic and aqueous history.
stops.question: Why sample igneous rocks? Their minerals can help date events and place the surrounding landscape in time.

stops.name: River delta
stops.body: A river once delivered sediment into a lake here. Layered outcrops such as Kodiak preserve a history that can be reconstructed from the arrangement of rock beds.
stops.factLabel: Years back into Mars’ watery past
stops.question: Fine sediment can bury and protect delicate chemical traces. That makes ancient lake deposits compelling places to investigate.

stops.name: Three Forks depot
stops.body: Perseverance placed ten sealed tubes on the surface as a backup sample depot. Other samples remain aboard the rover for potential future recovery.
stops.question: Collecting is only the first step: bringing samples to Earth requires a separate mission. A future return is not guaranteed.

stops.name: Crater rim
stops.body: Climbing to the rim opens another chapter: rocks shaped by the impact and material that may predate the crater itself. Geology becomes a journey backward through time.
stops.factLabel: A wider window into the ancient crust
stops.question: Compare a rock’s chemistry with where it lies. A sample without its geological context tells only part of the story.

timeline.title: Next stop: Mars
timeline.body: An Atlas V launches the Mars 2020 spacecraft on its interplanetary journey.

timeline.title: Seven minutes of descent
timeline.body: A heat shield, parachute and rocket-powered sky crane deliver the rover to Jezero.

timeline.title: A companion takes flight
timeline.body: Ingenuity makes the first powered, controlled flight on another planet. It ultimately completes 72 flights, ending in January 2024.

timeline.title: A cache for the future
timeline.body: The tenth tube completes the Three Forks backup depot, preserving an option for possible sample recovery.

perseverance.scienceTitle: What can a rock tell us?
perseverance.scienceIntro: The mission connects landscapes, microscopic textures and chemistry. No single observation tells the whole story.

science.title: A lake written in stone
science.body: Layered sediments reveal deposition by water; igneous rocks record a different part of the crater’s history. Comparing them helps reconstruct how this environment changed.

science.title: A question, not a verdict
science.body: Organic compounds and intriguing mineral patterns can have biological or non-biological origins. Potential biosignatures need multiple lines of evidence and careful testing before they can establish ancient life.

science.title: Making oxygen on Mars
science.body: The MOXIE technology experiment extracted oxygen from the carbon-dioxide-rich atmosphere. Its 16 runs produced 122 grams in total, demonstrating a step toward making resources locally.

perseverance.instrumentIntro: Seven primary instruments work alongside the drill and sample-handling system. Open each group to see how the measurements complement one another.

instruments.name: Mastcam-Z + SuperCam
instruments.body: Stereo zoom cameras survey the landscape; remote spectroscopy investigates rock chemistry.

instruments.name: PIXL + SHERLOC
instruments.body: A pair of arm-mounted instruments maps elements, minerals and organic compounds at small scales.

instruments.name: RIMFAX + MEDA
instruments.body: Ground-penetrating radar probes below the wheels while weather sensors study conditions above them.

instruments.name: MOXIE
instruments.body: A completed technology demonstration tested oxygen production from the Martian atmosphere.

instrumentDetails: Mastcam-Z provides colour stereo views and zoom. SuperCam uses a laser and several spectroscopic techniques to examine targets from a distance, helping the team choose where to investigate next.
PIXL uses X-ray fluorescence to map chemical elements. SHERLOC uses ultraviolet Raman and fluorescence spectroscopy to investigate minerals and organics; WATSON adds close-up images for context.
RIMFAX sends radar pulses into the ground and measures reflections from subsurface structures. MEDA records temperature, wind, pressure, dust and other environmental conditions.
MOXIE used high-temperature electrochemistry to separate oxygen from carbon dioxide. It completed its demonstration in 2023; it was an experiment, not an astronaut life-support system.

communication.title: Why you cannot joystick a Mars rover
communication.body: Radio signals take minutes to cross the distance between Earth and Mars. Teams send plans; the rover executes sequences and uses onboard autonomy to help navigate. Much of its science data is relayed through Mars orbiters.
communication.note: Try an example distance in the calculator. The result is a light-time estimate, not a current measurement or a complete command-response schedule.

faq.question: Has Perseverance discovered life on Mars?
faq.answer: No confirmed discovery of Martian life is established by the evidence described here. The rover investigates ancient habitability and potential biosignatures; promising chemistry is a reason for further study.

faq.question: Will the samples definitely reach Earth?
faq.answer: They are collected for possible future return. Recovery, launch from Mars and delivery to Earth require additional spacecraft and an approved mission plan; Perseverance cannot bring them back itself.

faq.question: Is Ingenuity still flying?
faq.answer: No. Its final flight was on 18 January 2024. Across 72 flights it demonstrated powered flight in Mars’ thin atmosphere and helped scout terrain for the rover.

cassini.name: Cassini–Huygens
cassini.intro: Saturn became a place with weather, changing rings, methane seas and a moon that sprays its hidden ocean into space. Cassini orbited the planet for 13 years; Huygens carried the adventure down to Titan’s surface.

status.title: Mission completed · 15 September 2017
status.body: Cassini ended with a planned plunge into Saturn. This is an exploration of its scientific legacy; the spacecraft no longer transmits data.

stats.label: Grand Finale
stats.note: Between Saturn and its inner rings

exploration.title: One mission. Many worlds.
exploration.intro: Choose a destination to uncover a different part of Cassini’s story: a giant atmosphere, a disk of ice, a hazy moon or a hidden ocean.
exploration.description: Illustrative view of Saturn, its rings, Titan and the plumes of Enceladus
exploration.note: Illustration, not an orbital reconstruction: sizes, distances, positions and the dotted path are not to scale or tied to a date.

stops.name: Saturn
stops.body: From seasonal change to enormous storms, the planet’s atmosphere became a long-term laboratory. Close final passes also probed its gravity and magnetic environment.
stops.question: A long mission sees what a flyby misses: how a planetary system changes with time.

stops.name: The rings
stops.body: The rings are countless orbiting particles, mostly water ice. Waves, gaps and small moonlets reveal gravity sculpting a disk in motion.
stops.question: During the Grand Finale, flying inside the rings let the team investigate Saturn and the ring system from a new vantage point.

stops.name: Titan
stops.body: Radar and infrared observations pierced the haze to reveal dunes, lakes and seas. Here the surface liquid cycle uses methane and ethane rather than water.
stops.question: Huygens landed here on 14 January 2005: the first landing on a world in the outer solar system.

stops.name: Enceladus
stops.body: Jets of water vapour and ice erupt near the south pole. Cassini sampled their chemistry and gathered evidence for a global ocean under the icy shell.
stops.question: Water, organic chemistry and possible chemical energy make habitability a compelling question. They do not establish that life exists.

timeline.title: The long way to Saturn
timeline.body: Launch begins a journey using gravity assists at Venus, Earth and Jupiter before Saturn arrival.

timeline.title: A new resident of Saturn
timeline.body: A braking burn makes Cassini the first spacecraft to orbit Saturn.

timeline.title: Huygens reaches Titan
timeline.body: ESA’s probe descends through the haze and sends measurements and surface images back via Cassini.

timeline.title: A purposeful finale
timeline.body: After 22 planet–ring dives, Cassini enters Saturn’s atmosphere, protecting the moons from a possible future collision.

cassini.scienceIntro: Cassini’s measurements continue to be studied. These three themes transformed our understanding of the Saturn system.

science.title: An ocean beneath the ice
science.body: Enceladus’ wobble and plume measurements support a global subsurface ocean. Hydrogen in the plume suggests water–rock reactions that could supply chemical energy.

science.title: Titan’s familiar, alien cycle
science.body: Liquids collect in lakes and seas on Titan, with methane playing a role analogous to water on Earth. Huygens and Cassini connected the surface landscape with its dense atmosphere.

science.title: A final experiment
science.body: Repeated dives through the ring gap brought measurements closer to Saturn than ever before. The finale traded the last of the spacecraft’s lifetime for a unique scientific perspective.

cassini.instrumentIntro: Cassini carried 12 science instruments; Huygens carried six. These groups highlight complementary ways the orbiter explored the system.

instruments.name: ISS · VIMS · CIRS · UVIS
instruments.body: Cameras and spectrometers studied appearance, composition and temperature across several wavelength ranges.

instruments.name: RADAR
instruments.body: Microwave observations revealed Titan’s surface beneath its thick atmospheric haze.

instruments.name: INMS + CDA
instruments.body: Gas and dust analysers sampled material encountered along the spacecraft’s path.

instruments.name: MAG · CAPS · MIMI · RPWS · RSS
instruments.body: Fields, particles, plasma waves and radio tracking connected the environment to the worlds within it.

instrumentDetails: ISS used narrow- and wide-angle cameras. VIMS mapped visible and infrared light; CIRS measured thermal infrared spectra; UVIS examined ultraviolet signatures, including changes during occultations.
RADAR transmitted microwaves and measured their echoes. It mapped terrain, measured heights and investigated how the surface reflected and emitted radiation.
INMS analysed neutral gas and ions, including material from Enceladus. The Cosmic Dust Analyzer investigated the composition and properties of individual dust and ice particles.
MAG measured magnetic fields; CAPS and MIMI studied charged particles; RPWS measured radio and plasma waves. RSS used radio signals to investigate gravity, atmospheres and rings.

communication.title: The last data crossed the void
communication.body: Cassini communicated through NASA’s Deep Space Network. Its final measurements travelled to Earth while the spacecraft was already gone: radio waves, like light, take time to cover interplanetary distances.
communication.note: There is no current Cassini link. The calculator uses an illustrative Earth–Saturn distance to show the delay a signal would experience.

faq.question: Where is Cassini now?
faq.answer: The spacecraft was destroyed in Saturn’s atmosphere on 15 September 2017. It is no longer in orbit and sends no telemetry. Its archived observations remain available for research.

faq.question: Were Cassini and Huygens the same spacecraft?
faq.answer: They travelled together but had different roles. The NASA-led Cassini orbiter explored the Saturn system; ESA’s Huygens probe separated and descended to Titan. ASI was a major mission partner.

faq.question: Did the mission find life on Enceladus?
faq.answer: No. It found evidence of an ocean and chemistry relevant to habitability. Finding an environment that could support life is different from detecting organisms.

cassini.galleryIntro: Visible-light mosaics, backlit plumes and infrared mapping each reveal a different aspect of the Saturn system.

gallery.title: The day Earth smiled
gallery.alt: Saturn backlit by the Sun, with its rings spread across a wide mosaic
gallery.body: On 19 July 2013, Cassini looked back from Saturn’s shadow. Earth appears as a tiny point in the larger original mosaic.

gallery.title: Fountains of Enceladus
gallery.alt: Backlit jets rising above the south polar limb of Enceladus
gallery.body: This 27 November 2005 image reveals fine material escaping from the moon. Backlighting makes the plume stand out against space.

gallery.title: Beneath Titan’s haze
gallery.alt: False-colour infrared view of Titan with surface regions visible through the haze
gallery.body: VIMS observations from 13 November 2015 map infrared wavelengths into visible colours. This is not how Titan would look to human eyes.
